text:
Since 2007, electricity prices in South Africa have gone up by about 900%, while prices in general rose by about 150%. How did Eskom end up so deep in debt that the government stepped in with up to R254 billion, and what does it cost you every month? Follow Nomsa (an illustration) from her prepaid units to the numbers behind them: Medupi and Kusile, load shedding, the Eskom Debt Relief Act, municipal arrears, Eskom's return to profit, and why selling less electricity means a higher price per unit. Then four simple ways to plan for it.

Key figures
- Kusile: budget about R80 billion, final cost more than R160 billion, more than 11 years late; last unit running from September 2025. Medupi and Kusile together: more than R300 billion over budget.
- 2023: close to 7,000 hours of load shedding. Eskom Debt Relief Act (2023): up to R254 billion over three years.
- Eskom, year to 31 March 2026: profit R30.3 billion (R14.0 billion the year before), net debt R313.3 billion, sales 178 TWh (down 6.2%), load shedding on 4 days (26 hours). Municipal arrears R111.6 billion at 31 March 2026 (R120.26 billion by 31 July 2026).
- Tariffs: Eskom direct customers +8.76% from 1 April 2026; Eskom's price to municipalities +9.01% from 1 July 2026; +8.83% proposed for 1 April 2027, pending final approval. NERSA corrected a R54.7 billion error in its own numbers.

About the example: Nomsa is an illustration. R1,000 a month of electricity x 1.09 = about R1,090 (about R90 a month more, almost R1,100 a year). On a R12,000 salary, R1,000 is 8.3%; with electricity +9% a year and pay +5% a year, it is about 10% after five years. Your municipality's tariff may differ.
